title: Type Inference
summary: TypeScript can often work out a value’s type from the code around it.

subtopics.title: Starting values
subtopics.explanation: An initial value can tell TypeScript a variable’s type. For example, `let count = 0` starts as a number. It is like labeling a jar from the first thing placed inside. TypeScript can then warn if code assigns a value that does not fit the inferred type. For example, a number initialized with zero is inferred as a number.

subtopics.title: Function results
subtopics.explanation: Function bodies and return expressions help TypeScript infer a return type. If every path returns a string, callers can use that knowledge. It is like learning what a machine produces by observing its output. Add an explicit return type when it makes a public contract easier to understand or maintain. For example, a helper that returns text can have its return type inferred from its branches.

subtopics.title: Changing a value
subtopics.explanation: Inference follows assignments and control flow, but the result can change depending on whether a variable may hold several values. It is like updating a label when the contents of a box change. Read inferred types in your editor when behavior is surprising, and prefer clear initialization over confusing later assignments. For example, a variable may have a union of types when later assignments allow several values.

subtopics.title: Public contracts
subtopics.explanation: Public functions and shared component props are contracts other code relies on. An explicit type can make that contract stable and easier to review. It is like printing the rules on a form before others fill it in. You do not need to annotate every local variable when the type is already obvious. For example, a public function can use an explicit return type to keep its contract stable.

subtopics.title: Outside data
subtopics.explanation: Inference cannot prove that a server response contains the shape you expect. TypeScript types disappear when the program runs. It is like writing a label on a delivery box without checking what arrived. Validate external data at runtime, then let TypeScript describe the validated result. For example, validate a parsed response before giving it a type annotation.

foundations.overview: Type inference is TypeScript’s ability to work out a value’s type from how it is created and used. It saves repeated annotations while still checking many mistakes. Think of it like recognizing an object from its contents. Inference is helpful for local values, but public interfaces and untrusted data often need explicit types or runtime validation.
foundations.whyItMatters: Inference keeps ordinary TypeScript code concise while preserving checks. Developers should add explicit types at shared boundaries and validate external inputs before trusting them.
foundations.browserPerspective: Inference happens entirely at compile time and changes nothing at runtime — whether a type was inferred or written by hand, it's erased the same way. The browser runs identical JavaScript either way.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Idiomatic code relies on inference constantly: inferred local variables, inferred return types, and contextually-typed callbacks in map/filter/reduce and event handlers. Annotations are reserved for function parameters and exported API surfaces.
foundations.businessImpact: Leaning on inference reduces boilerplate and keeps code readable, while still catching bugs — so teams move faster without sacrificing safety. Misunderstanding widening can cause confusing type errors that slow people down.
foundations.engineeringImpact: A clear annotate-the-boundaries, infer-the-internals convention keeps diffs small and code consistent. It also makes refactors safer: change an internal value and its inferred type updates automatically, while boundary annotations keep contracts stable.
foundations.performanceImpact: No runtime impact. Heavy reliance on complex inferred types can marginally affect type-checking speed in large projects, but for everyday code the effect is negligible.
commonUseCases: Letting local variables take their type from their initializer
Omitting return-type annotations on simple internal functions
Relying on contextual typing for map/filter callbacks and event handlers
Using const to get precise literal types for constants

commonMisconceptions.myth: You must annotate every variable for TypeScript to be safe.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Inference types most expressions automatically; annotating everything is redundant. Annotate boundaries, infer internals.

commonMisconceptions.myth: const and let infer the same type for the same value.
commonMisconceptions.reality: const infers the narrow literal type (because it can't be reassigned); let widens to the general type.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Inference checks data received from an API at runtime.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Inference only reasons about source code; the response needs runtime validation.

commonMisconceptions.myth: An explicit annotation always makes a type more precise.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A broad annotation can discard useful inferred detail, so add one when it clarifies intent.

visualExplorer.title: How TypeScript infers a type
visualExplorer.caption: Follow the clues the compiler uses to deduce a type, and where it asks for help.

config.intro: Trace how the compiler infers types and when it needs an annotation.

steps.name: Look at the initializer
steps.detail: const total = 5 gives the compiler a value to read; it infers a type from it.

steps.name: Apply widening rules
steps.detail: const keeps the literal (5); let widens to the general type (number) because it can be reassigned.

steps.name: Infer function returns
steps.detail: From a function's return statements, the compiler infers the return type — no annotation needed.

steps.name: Use the context
steps.detail: In arr.map(n => ...), the array's element type flows in, so n is inferred without annotation.

steps.name: Detect missing clues
steps.detail: With no value to read (an empty array or bare parameter), inference falls back to any or asks for a type.

steps.name: Annotate the boundary
steps.detail: You supply types at parameters and exported APIs; inference handles the internals.

codeLab.title: Annotate boundaries, infer internals
codeLab.instructions: Annotate only the function parameters (the boundary) and let TypeScript infer the local variable and return type. Don't over-annotate. discount(100, 0.2) should log 80.
hints: Annotate price and rate as ': number' — parameters have no value to infer from.
Leave 'off' and the return type alone; the compiler infers number for both.

keyTakeaways: An initial value can tell TypeScript a variable’s type.
Function bodies and return expressions help TypeScript infer a return type.
Inference follows assignments and control flow, but the result can change depending on whether a variable may hold several values.
Public functions and shared component props are contracts other code relies on.
Inference cannot prove that a server response contains the shape you expect.
